newsitem.title: CANADA: Gulf Canada agrees to buy Stampeder Exploration.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Canada agrees to buy Stampeder Exploration.

text.p: Stampeder Exploration Ltd. agreed on Monday to a C$1 billion ($720 million) friendly merger with Gulf Canada Resources Ltd. in a move that would rescue Stampeder from a crippling cash crunch.

Calgary-based Gulf, which last month was outbid by PanCanadian Petroleum Ltd. for heavy oil producer CS Resources Ltd., said it would offer 0.69124 of a Gulf share for each Stampeder share. The price included about C$300 million ($219 million) of Stampeder debt.

The board of Calgary-based Stampeder, also a large producer of heavy oil in western Canada, agreed to pay Gulf a C$20 million ($14.4 million) breakup fee if a rival bid was successful in winning the company, a situation Gulf Chief Executive J.P. Bryan said was unlikely.
Gulf said the offer represented a 31 percent premium over Stampeder's closing stock price of C$5.70 ($4.10) Friday.

Stampeder Chief Executive Jeff Tonken conceded his once high-flying company sought out Gulf about two weeks ago when it became clear it did not have the money to fund its capital spending programme after a failed equity issue.
The company's stock rose to C$8.15 ($5.95) in January after it made three major acquisitions in 1996, the last of which was the C$500 million ($365 million) takeover of Morgan Hydrocarbons.

But Stampeder fell out of favour with investors, who unloaded the stock in June when Tonken announced a share issue to fund an C$85 million ($62 million) increase in second-half spending, mostly targeting heavy crude oil prospects. Stampeder scrapped the offering after its stock price slumped.

"Because our equity issue failed, we were left with two choices," Tonken said in a conference call. "One choice was to downsize the company and sell assets so we could continue to drill. We did not want to do that."
Instead, the company approached Gulf, which was still in the market for a heavy oil producing company after the loss of CS to PanCanadian.

Bryan said his plans for Stampeder were similar to those for CS, which included folding in the target company's heavy oil assets with Gulf's heavy oil and oil sands operations to form a new company, which could go public and acquire similar assets worldwide.

But Stampeder offered the benefit of other operations in light oil and natural gas, which made up about 55 percent of the company, as well as a marketing business that could be merged with Gulf's, he said.

Bryan said Gulf's offer valued Stampeder's oil and gas reserves at C$5 ($3.65) to C$5.50 ($4.02) per barrel of oil equivalent. The company had about 93 million barrels of proved reserves at the end of 1996 and current production was about 32,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day.

He also said Gulf planned to sell its large Zama/Virgo oil and gas property in northern Alberta for estimated proceeds of up to C$400 million ($292 million), with the proceeds to be directed at paying down debt acquired in the Stampeder deal.

Stampeder stock topped actives on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Monday, up C$1.20 at C$6.90 on 5.4 million shares. Its New York Stock Exchange-listed shares were up 94 cents at $5 in consolidated late trading.
Gulf Canada stock in Toronto was off C60 cents at C$10.20 on volume of 2.4 million shares. In New York, Gulf was down 44 cents at $7.375.
